extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of chemistry (historical/early-modern chemistry readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and tables for naming neutral salts (nomenclature nouvelle), ordering acid–base combinations by affinity, and experimental procedures to obtain and handle various acids (phosphoreux/phosphorique, carbonique, muriatique, nitro-muriatique, fluorique, boracique, arsenique, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nomenclature nouvelle for phosphorous acid salts
rubrics_metrics.description: Table labelled "NOMENCLATURE NOUVELLE" listing "Noms des bases" and corresponding "Noms des sels neutres" (e.g. "Phosphite de chaux", "Phosphite de baryte", "Phosphite de magnésie", etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the proposed 'nomenclature nouvelle' to name neutral salts of the acid phosphoreux as 'phosphite de [base]'. Note: the existence of some 'phosphites métalliques' is uncertain ("L'existence des phosphites métalliques n'est pas encore absolument certaine"). Many of these salts had not previously been named.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nomenclature nouvelle for phosphoric acid salts
rubrics_metrics.description: Table "NOMENCLATURE NOUVELLE" for combinations of "l'Acide phosphorique" with bases giving names like "Phosphate de chaux", "Phosphate de baryte", etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the new nomenclature consistently: neutral salts of acide phosphorique are named 'phosphate de [base]'. The text notes many of these salts were known only recently and had not yet been named historically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order combinations by chemical affinity
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple tables present combinations of an acid (radical) with 'les bases salifiables' "dans l'ordre de leur affinité avec cet acide".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When tabulating or reasoning about acid–base combinations, arrange bases in descending order of affinity for the acid. The ordering is used as the organizing principle for the various 'TABLEAU' entries across different acids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method to obtain pure acide phosphorique (phosphoric acid)
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain by burning phosphorus ('prendre du phosphore en nature, & de le faire brûler') under glass bells whose interiors have been moistened with distilled water; phosphorus absorbs about 2.5 times its weight of oxygen in the operation. Alternatively, burn on mercury to obtain white flocons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed experimental notes: perform combustion under glass bell with distilled water to collect the acid; burning on mercury yields concrete white flakes which are extremely hygroscopic. After formation, the acid may appear partly solid and partly liquid in a tubulated retort if prepared via nitric acid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method to obtain acide phosphoreux (phosphorous acid)
rubrics_metrics.description: Produce by allowing phosphorus to burn extremely slowly and letting condensate collect in a funnel into a flask; the less-oxygenated acid (acide phosphoreux) is obtained as it absorbs humidity and runs into the bottle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acide phosphoreux forms under very slow combustion and is readily oxidized to acide phosphorique upon extended exposure to air. It can be collected as a liquid by providing a funnel and flask to capture deliquesced condensate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using nitric acid to make phosphoric acid (alternative method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce small pieces of phosphorus into slightly heated concentrated nitric acid in a tubulated retort (cornue tubulée); phosphorous dissolves with effervescence; nitrous gas escapes as brilliant vapours; continue adding phosphorus until it ceases to dissolve, then increase heat to drive off remaining nitric acid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This yields acide phosphorique in the retort, partly as a concrete form and partly liquid. The procedure specifies a cornue tubulée with a crystal stopper, and care to continue until phosphorus no longer dissolves and to drive off residual nitric acid by raising temperature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method to liberate acide carbonique (carbonic acid/CO2) from carbonates
rubrics_metrics.description: Pour concentrated sulfuric acid (or any acid with greater affinity for lime) onto carbonate-bearing materials (chalk, marble, calcareous stones) to produce vigorous effervescence; the evolved gas is carbonic acid (carbon dioxide).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The effervescence indicates gas liberation. Carbonic acid exists naturally as a gas under ordinary temperature and pressure and resists condensation under applied cooling/pressure; it dissolves in water roughly in equal volumes producing a very weak acid. Alternative source: fermentation of sugary matter (contains some alcohol).

rubrics_metrics.name: Artificial formation of acide carbonique
rubrics_metrics.description: Form carbonic acid by burning charcoal in oxygen or by combining powdered charcoal with a metallic oxide in proper proportions; oxygen of the oxide combines with carbon producing carbonic acid gas and freeing the metal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides an artificial production route; historical attribution to Black for early knowledge. Notes on the impracticality of decomposing carbonic acid cheaply by simple affinities but the possibility via double affinities (biological precedent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Method to obtain acide muriatique (hydrochloric acid)
rubrics_metrics.description: Produce by treating seawater salt (sel marin) with concentrated sulfuric acid in a tubulated retort (cornue), using a Woulfe-style apparatus of connected bottles to absorb the evolved gas; introduce sulfuric acid into the retort and immediately close with crystal stopper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acide muriatique exists only as a gas at ordinary temperature/pressure and must be absorbed by water; the set of connected bottles (Woulfe) collects the acid in aqueous solution. Avoid using nitric acid as it is volatile and would mix during distillation. The procedure specifies roughly one part concentrated sulfuric acid to two parts salt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acide muriatique oxygéné (oxy-muriatic acid) formation and hazards
rubrics_metrics.description: Acide muriatique distilled over metal oxides (manganese oxide, lead oxide, or mercury oxide) yields an 'acide muriatique oxygéné' which cannot exist free except as a gas and is less readily absorbed by water; if over-saturated it precipitates concretely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Berthollet showed that the oxy-muriatic acid can combine with many salifiable bases; salts formed from it may detonate with carbon and several metals, releasing large caloric leading to dangerous explosions. Handle with extreme caution; recognize increased reactivity and explosive risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acide nitro-muriatique (aqua regia) composition and behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: Formed by mixing acide nitrique and acide muriatique; its radicals unite to produce an acid 'à deux bases' with properties not belonging to either acid separately, notably the ability to dissolve gold and platinum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In dissolutions, metals oxidize before dissolving and emit a peculiar nitro-muriatic gas with very disagreeable, toxic fumes that corrode iron instruments and produce acidic water on absorption. The author treats acide nitro-muriatique as an acid with two bases (following Berthollet) rather than as oxidized muriatic acid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acide fluorique preparation and material constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain hydrofluoric acid by putting fluate de chaux (spath fluor) in a lead retort and adding sulfuric acid; collect the acid by absorption into water in a lead receiver or via mercury pneumatics, because acide fluorique is gaseous at ordinary conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use metal vessels (lead) because acide fluorique dissolves glass and siliceous earth and even volatilizes them into the gas. Historical notes: Margraff, Liancourt, Schéele credited for discoveries. The apparatus and vessel material choice are essential precautions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acide boracique (boric acid) separation from borax
rubrics_metrics.description: Dissolve borax in boiling water, filter hot solution, then add sulfuric acid (or any acid with higher affinity for soda) to precipitate acide boracique; cool to crystallize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acide boracique is soluble in water and alcohol, gives a green color to alcohol flames (historically mistaken for copper), and its radical is unknown. Purification by one or two crystallizations is recommended; production method depends on using an acid that has greater affinity for sodium than boracic acid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notation on recently discovered salts and older nomenclature
rubrics_metrics.description: Many of the salts listed in the tables are known only from recent years and lacked 'nomenclature ancienne'; commentators note previous authors' names (e.g., Morveau, Bergman, Fourcroy) and historical epithets (e.g., 'aérée', 'acide crayeux').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When introducing new names, acknowledge historical terminology and the novelty of certain salts. The text provides correspondences between new and older names (where available) and explains that some combinations were unknown to earlier chemists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical cautions about reagent choice and volatility
rubrics_metrics.description: General experimental cautions repeated in the observations: do not use volatile acids (e.g., nitric acid) when they would contaminate or volatilize and mix with the desired product; choose acids with greater affinity to displace bases; be mindful of gases that cannot be condensed and must be absorbed by water or collected pneumatically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: avoid nitric acid when producing muriatic acid because it would volatilize and blend during distillation; use sulfuric acid to free carbonic or boracic acids from carbonates/borax; gas collection apparatus (Woulfe bottles, lead retorts, mercury pneumatics) must be chosen according to the acid's chemical effects and physical state.
